titleText.es: Ahora en serio: hay un montón de vida inteligente, sólo que no está gritando en todas direcciones en el puñado de frecuencias que miramos.
titleText.en: But seriously, there's loads of intelligent life. It's just not screaming constantly in all directions on the handful of frequencies we search.

excludedUnits.rationale: This is the unchanged surname of astronomer Frank Drake, not a Spanish lexical item.

regions.labelEs: NÚMERO DE CIVILIZACIONES QUE SE COMUNICAN EN NUESTRA GALAXIA.

applications.exampleEs: CIVILIZACIONES QUE SE COMUNICAN EN NUESTRA GALAXIA
applications.explanationEn: Que connects civilizaciones to the complete information that follows; se comunican supplies the action, and en nuestra galaxia supplies its location.
Se matches the plural group, and comunican is the plural present-time form of comunicar.

regions.labelEs: PROBABILIDAD DE QUE LA VIDA DE UN PLANETA SE HAGA INTELIGENTE

applications.exampleEs: PROBABILIDAD DE QUE LA VIDA DE UN PLANETA SE HAGA INTELIGENTE
applications.explanationEn: Probabilidad de que introduces an uncertain outcome. La vida de un planeta names what may change, haga is the special possibility form, and inteligente names its possible new state.
Se and haga form the possibility version of hacerse, and inteligente names the resulting state.

applications.explanationEn: Adecuados uses masculine plural -os to match planetas; por sistema solar is intervening rate information rather than part of that agreement.
Adecuados matches the plural thing being evaluated, and para introduces the complete use or condition that follows.

excludedUnits.rationale: This is the unchanged personal name of astronomer Frank Drake, not Spanish lexical vocabulary.

applications.exampleEs: GILIPOLLECES DE FRANK DRAKE QUE UNO ESTÁ DISPUESTO A TRAGARSE
applications.explanationEn: The words before que name the gilipolleces and their source; que then opens the information about what uno is willing to do with them.
Está supplies the state, dispuesto marks willingness, a introduces the action, and tragarse stays in its unchanged dictionary form.

cards.answerEn: a framework that multiplies estimated factors to approximate how many extraterrestrial civilizations might communicate in the Milky Way
cards.noteEn: Astronomer Frank Drake introduced the framework in 1961. Its factors concern stars, planets, life, intelligence, communication, and how long detectable civilizations last; their uncertain values make the result an estimate, not a measured count.
De can join an invention, theorem, or named object to the person whose name it bears. English may instead use an adjective based on that name.

example.en: We study Newton's laws.

cards.questionEn: How do you add information about a named person or thing using “who,” “that,” or “which”?
cards.answerEn: Put que after the person or thing, then add a verb and the information about it.
cards.noteEn: Que links the added description to the person or thing before it. It does not change for masculine, feminine, singular, or plural nouns. The added part needs a verb: la casa que vimos means “the house that we saw.”

example.es: La casa que vimos es azul.
example.en: The house that we saw is blue.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; helps comunicarse mean ‘to communicate’
cards.noteEn: Comunicarse uses a short marker that matches who communicates: me comunico, te comunicas, se comunica, nos comunicamos, os comunicáis, or se comunican. The marker stays directly before a normal changed form of comunicar.

example.en: We communicate by email.

cards.promptEs: comunicarse (con alguien o por un medio)
cards.questionEn: How do you say that people communicate or get in touch?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching short marker with a form of comunicar: me comunico, te comunicas, se comunica, nos comunicamos, os comunicáis, or se comunican.
cards.noteEn: The short marker changes with the person or group, and comunicar changes for that same person or group. Con can introduce who receives the communication; por can introduce the medium used.

example.en: We communicate by text messages.

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce an outcome whose probability or chance is being discussed?
cards.answerEn: Use probabilidad de que, then describe the uncertain outcome with the special verb form Spanish uses for possibilities.
cards.noteEn: This special form is called the subjunctive. It presents the outcome as possible rather than asserted as a fact: ordinary llueve changes to llueva, and se hace changes to se haga. The plus sign in the prompt means “followed by.”

example.es: Hay poca probabilidad de que llueva.
example.en: There is little chance that it will rain.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; connects probabilidad to a following que clause
cards.noteEn: Spanish says probabilidad de que before a full possible outcome. Natural English usually says “probability that,” absorbing de rather than translating it as a separate “of.”

example.es: Hay poca probabilidad de que nieve.
example.en: There is little chance that it will snow.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; Spanish uses la before a general abstract idea such as vida
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses el or la when discussing an idea in general, while English uses the bare noun without “the.” The article still matches the noun: la vida, la paciencia, el tiempo.

example.en: Patience is important.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; helps hacerse mean ‘to become’
cards.noteEn: With a describing word, hacerse can present a gradual or noticeable change in the subject's state.

example.es: Los días se hacen más largos.
example.en: The days are getting longer.

cards.questionEn: How can you say that a person or thing becomes or gradually grows a certain way?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of hacerse followed by the word that describes the new state.
cards.noteEn: The short marker and hacer form change with the subject: me hago, te haces, se hace, nos hacemos, and so on. The describing word matches the person or thing in number and, when its form changes, gender.

example.es: Las tardes se hacen más cortas.
example.en: The afternoons are getting shorter.

cards.answerEn: becomes (special form of hacerse after an uncertain possibility)
cards.noteEn: Haga is a changed form of hacer. With se and a describing word, it belongs to hacerse, “to become.” After an expression of uncertainty or probability, Spanish often changes se hace to se haga.

example.es: Es posible que se haga famoso.
example.en: It is possible that he will become famous.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: Por can introduce the unit used to divide or distribute a quantity. The unit after por stays singular when it means “for each one.”

example.en: There are two books per student.

cards.noteEn: Adecuados ends in -os because it describes a masculine plural noun. The other matching forms are adecuado, adecuada, and adecuadas.

example.en: They are suitable places for children.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something is suitable for a particular use, person, or situation?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of adecuado, then para, then name the use, person, situation, or action.
cards.noteEn: Adecuado changes its ending to match what is suitable: adecuado, adecuada, adecuados, or adecuadas. If an action follows para, that action stays in its unchanged dictionary form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The slash marks alternatives, and the plus sign means “followed by.”

example.es: Esta sala es adecuada para estudiar.
example.en: This room is suitable for studying.

cards.answerEn: for; introduces what something is suitable for
cards.noteEn: After adecuado or a matching form such as adecuada or adecuados, para introduces the intended use, person, situation, or action.

example.es: Esta mesa es adecuada para niños.
example.en: This table is suitable for children.

cards.promptEs: factor B_s en esta parodia de la ecuación de Drake
cards.answerEn: the comic's invented “bullshit” factor: how much of Drake's speculation someone is willing to accept
cards.noteEn: B_s is not part of the real Drake equation. The comic turns skepticism about uncertain inputs into one more fake multiplier, making the amount of accepted nonsense determine the answer.
Gilipolleces is a strongly informal and vulgar plural. The singular gilipollez can mean one stupid or nonsensical thing.

example.en: Stop talking bullshit.

cards.answerEn: by; from (identifying the creator or source)
cards.noteEn: De can connect a work, statement, or piece of commentary to the person who created or supplied it. Natural English often uses “by” rather than literal “of.”

example.en: I read an article by Marta.

cards.noteEn: Uno can stand for an unspecified person rather than the number one. Natural English often uses generic “you” or “people” instead of formal “one.”

example.en: You never know.

cards.promptEs: estar dispuesto/dispuesta a + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is willing or prepared to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar, then a matching form of dispuesto, then a, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes for the person and time. Dispuesto changes to match that person in gender and number. The action after a remains in its dictionary form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The slash marks alternatives, and the plus sign means “followed by.”

example.en: Ana is willing to help.

cards.noteEn: Dispuesto changes to dispuesta, dispuestos, or dispuestas to match the person or group being described. A following a can introduce the action that person is willing to do.

example.en: Luis is willing to wait.

cards.answerEn: to (linking a verb to the following infinitive)
to swallow; to buy or accept uncritically
cards.noteEn: Tragarse can describe literal swallowing, but it also means accepting a claim or story too readily. The attached se is part of this dictionary form.

example.en: I don't buy that rumor.
